name: Municipality
description: A village or town office: the official notice board with its archive, documents such as regulations and forms, events, the council and staff, and residents' questions, with facts about the mayor, population and office contacts.

questions.question: Who is the mayor?
questions.help: The full name with the title as used officially.

questions.question: How many inhabitants does the municipality have?
questions.help: The latest official figure, as a number; update it when the statistics office publishes a new one.

questions.question: What is the area of the municipality in hectares?
What is the e-mail address of the filing office for official submissions?
What is the ID of the office's electronic mailbox (data box)?
questions.help: Leave it empty if your country has no such system.

questions.question: In which year was the municipality first mentioned in writing?
When and where does the council meet?
questions.help: For example "every second Thursday of the month at 18:00 in the council chamber".

audit.message: Post the current official notices on the notice board – an electronic notice board is usually required of a municipality; check what your law says.
Nothing has been posted on the notice board for two months – check that every current notice is there.
Publish the regulations, forms and the budget as documents so that residents can download the current version.
Name the mayor – residents want to know who represents the municipality.
Add the office hours in Business details – residents check them before they come.
Publish an accessibility statement – public bodies are usually required to have one; check what applies to you.

claude: Residents come to a municipal site for the official notice board, office hours and contacts, forms and regulations, news and what is happening – these belong on the home page, before history and photos. Official notices must keep their posting and takedown dates and are never deleted or hidden once posted; put every notice into the notice board collection, not into news or pages. Write in plain, neutral official language, equally for every resident; accessibility matters here, so use proper headings, descriptive link texts and alternative texts for every image, and offer documents as accessible files where possible. Never invent population figures, history, names of officials, meeting dates or budgets – ask the office and cite the source where a figure is published. Where a legal duty may apply (notice board, accessibility statement, information duties), say that it should be checked with the office rather than stating it as law.
